case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: Well, the  -- I'm sorry. The  --the defendant in this case is the district attorney, right?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: That's correct, Your Honor.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: And so would you agree that you have to show that what you seek, obtaining access to evidence for DNA testing, would be redressed by a declaratory  judgment that applies to the district attorney?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: We would have to --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: Has to be redressed through the district attorney?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Yes, Your Honor. However, the district attorney isn't bound by a declaratory judgment. What they would be bound by is the res judicata effect of the declaratory judgment on the parties. Should the district attorney choose not to give the DNA, we could then go back to state court and would have the declaratory judgment in hand, and the state court would be bound by the determination of the --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: Well, let me ask it this way. Is this  -- do you think the standing argument is different because you sought a declaratory judgment as opposed to an injunction?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Well, we were not able to seek an injunction. We tried to seek an injunction in this case, and  --and we lost. But we seek a declaratory judgment just like Rodney Reed sought a declaratory judgment, just like  --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: Well, would there be standing if you sought an injunction?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: There would be  --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: That you'd  -- you would to have show that you could vindicate what you seek by means of an order directed to the defendant, that is, the attorney general?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Yes. We would have sand  --standing if we sought an injunction. If the court had power to order the district attorney  --attorney to turn over the evidence, we would have standing to seek that.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: And some of the  --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: And you asked for that, didn't you?  I mean, in -- if I read paragraph 97 of your complaint, that asks, among other things, for an injunction to the district attorney, is that correct?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: That's correct, Your Honor.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: And is there still a possibility of getting that or not?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: No, Your Honor.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: Because?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Well, we lost that  -- we  -- we weren't granted relief on that claim and we did not appeal that claim, and so we 're not seeking relief on that claim through an appellate process.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Some of the awkwardness, I suppose, of the procedure here stems really from Osborne and Skinner itself in that it recognized a 1983 right in a context where, arguably, habeas, that, certainly, the dissenters pointed that out, but we are where we are on that, and that seems to me to -- to undergird some of the awkwardness here.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: I couldn't agree more, Your Honor. I think it's a  --it is a bit of a sort of awkward construct to sue the district attorney when it's a  --discretionary based on a declaratory judgment, but that's what Osborne and Skinner and now Reed have said that you do. And the idea, I believe, is that the declaratory judgment, while it wouldn't bind or  -- it wouldn't force the district attorney to turn over the evidence, it would be a legal ruling from a federal court that the procedures in question were unconstitutional. And  we believe that the district attorney, if they were ordered by the Court to turn it over, wouldn't  --would, of course, turn it over in the state court or that they wouldn't rely on an unconstitutional statute.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Now, when you get back to state court  -- say you won and the Fifth Circuit said it's a procedural due process problem. You get back to state court, it's not turned over by the prosecutor. The state court would presumably go through the Chapter 64 proceeding, right, and -- and figure out, okay, does this  --is he entitled to the testing, or would it be, in essence, harmless error even if he were entitled to the testing, which is akin to what they've done already, I guess.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Well, our position, Your Honor, is that the CCA has never actually decided whether Mr. Gutierrez should get testing  under a constitutional version of the statute.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Mm-hmm.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: You are correct. We would go back to state court. We would file another Chapter 64 motion with a constitutional -- asking for the court to apply the constitutional determination made by the federal district court.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: And by "constitutional," just so I'm under  --you mean a system where you can bring a Chapter 64 not just to show you 're innocent of -- innocent of the underlying crime but that you're ineligible for the death penalty?  That's where the procedural due process issue is?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: It's that plus more, though, because it's not simply sort of slapping on death eligibility to the current Chapter 64 statute, because the current Chapter 64 statute is designed to figure out who should get DNA testing to determine who's actually innocent of the crime. So all of the procedures that are baked into Chapter 64, by -- by necessity, it's logical, I'm sure Texas had reasons for doing this, are designed to decide who should get DNA testing to show they're actually innocent.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Ms. Fisher, that  -- that's -- I'd just like to follow up on that because, in the June order from the TCCA, looking at Joint Appendix 478 and 479  --and I'm sure you're familiar with it  --they say, even if 64 -- Chapter 64 does apply to the question of death eligibility, that your client still wouldn't receive relief because, effectively, as Justice Kavanaugh pointed out, harmless error here. And -- and  --and what do we do about that?  They seem to have anticipated this -- this very issue because it was before the district court, though, you're right, the Fifth Circuit came out the other way. But this issue's been lingering in the case for a long time, and the TCCA has said now, I think twice, that whether 64 applies to the death stage -- death penalty stage or not, your client would not seek  --be eligible for relief. Thoughts?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Yes, Your Honor. The provision that -- when the CCA made that ruling, they weren't considering the due process violation found by the district court, which,  again, goes beyond simply asking does Chapter 64 in its current iteration allow for death ineligibility. What the due process violation found by the district court addresses are the  procedures within Chapter 64 and whether or not they're adequate to vindicate the right --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Well, I  -- I -- I'm sorry to interrupt you there, but the TCCA said, given the evidence presented, the statute did not operate unconstitutionally as to Appellant because  --harmless error, effectively. I'm summarizing, but that's the gist of  it. Are you saying your due process claim would preclude a court from applying a harmless error test?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: No, Your Honor. What I am saying is that that determination by the Texas CCA was not saying that the procedures in Chapter 64 are inadequate and we need to look how  -- what -- what will make them adequate . By limiting their determination to the record evidence -- and you'll see -- I -- I'm sure you've seen -- they simply sort of cut and  paste and recite the two sentences, the "even if" determination  --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Yeah.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: -- back from 2011.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: That they'd previously said, yeah.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Right. That determination does not actually consider how to make Chapter 64 a test that will vindicate the right in a way that isn't illusory, and that's because the  --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: I guess I'm struggling to understand what you would have them do besides say 64 applies to the death penalty stage. What's your due process complaint besides that?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: They would have to consider a broader scope of evidence. The key words in that "even if" holding that they had or the  -- what Your Honor cited is when they say they limit it to the trial evidence or the record evidence. That limitation is a limitation that was designed with the procedures in Chapter 64 that were supposed to figure out who's going to get DNA to show they're actually innocent. And  that's because, if you add DNA to the mix of trial evidence, you can pretty easily figure out if DNA is going to show someone is actually innocent.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Well, but that's -- that's added to this, and you're sort of figuring out, well, how -- how much is the weight of the evidence. Would it -- how much would it take?  Like a tiny thimbleful of additional evidence?  I mean, how is a court supposed to figure that out?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Well, this -- the -- a petitioner could go before a federal court and argue a due process claim because they had just a little bit of new evidence, but I would suspect that that petitioner would be turned down because of a 12(b)(6) ruling. So it would still have to be meaningful evidence. No court has considered this evidence, and it really is the scope of evidence that's critical here because those prior decisions by the CCA didn't look at the right that was being squelched in the due  --in the habeas petition.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: When  you're bringing  --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: But I thought  --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: Are -- are --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: -- when you're bring --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: No, go ahead.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: When you're bringing the new claim, you're going to argue, I gather, and have argued that there's more than just DNA since the trial?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: That's exactly it. To file a claim that a petitioner is death-ineligible --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: And can you explain what that is?  I'd be interested in you listing what that is.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Yes. So what Mr. Gutierrez would need to present in his claim to show that he's death-ineligible would be two different types of new evidence. It would need the DNA because he'd have to show that he wasn't actually in the home and that he didn't actually kill the decedent. But he'd also have to show evidence to show that he wasn't a major participant of the crime. This is the Enmund/Tison liability. That evidence is not going to be in the form of record evidence or DNA. That's going to be newly developed evidence like we have found, which would include things like -- and this is not an exhaustive list  --but it would include things like a statement from the primary suspect, Avel Cuellar's nephew, that Mr. Cuellar, who everyone in the trailer park believed had killed her when this happened, had actually approached him about committing this very crime two weeks before the crime and that after the crime he had hundreds of thousands of dollars buried in the trailer park near his home, and there were hundreds of thousands of dollars that were not accounted for after this crime occurred.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: But --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: They would have to do a lie detector test that the -- wasn't discovered by trial counsel. All things that would go to his role because Mr. Gutierrez was tried under the law of parties.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: What does that have to do with the question whether the limitation in the Texas statute to evidence that shows innocence as opposed to death ineligibility is constitutional?  That's a separate question, isn't it? Whether it's  --you're -- are you arguing that it's a violation of his constitutional rights for Texas to say that in this context  --for the Texas courts to say, in this context, we are only considering evidence that's already in the record?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: No, Your Honor. We wouldn't argue it separately because it's part of the procedures that don't  --that make the right to file the habeas illusory, and if I may explain. The limitation is designed to limit the access to evidence to people who can show they're actually innocent who weren't also a party to the crime. The law of parties actually really is critical here because the reason Mr. Gutierrez was told by the CCA that he couldn't access evidence to show that he didn't actually kill the decedent  --or, excuse me, wasn't in the house was because he was  still -- there was enough record evidence to show he was still a party to the crime. And so it didn't really matter if he was the person who killed the decedent or was in the home. There was enough evidence to show he was a party. And if he was a party, then DNA evidence wouldn't exonerate him.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: Well, I understand  --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: Counsel  --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: -- I understand all that. But, when you talk about this other evidence, you're raising all sorts of other issues. It's -- is it newly discovered evidence?  Could you have had access to this evidence at the time of trial?  Does it meet all of the other requirements of newly discovered evidence?  To what extent, if any, is any of that constitutionally required?  Your own -- that doesn't seem to have anything to do with the question whether this differentiation under Texas law between evidence that shows lack of guilt and evidence that shows death ineligibility is constitutional.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Justice Alito, adding DNA evidence simply to the record evidence will  almost never show that someone's not a major participant of the crime, which is what someone needs to show to show that they're death-ineligible. It's that other part of the evidence that I was addressing with Justice  Kavanaugh. And so, because the 5(a)(3) section, this habeas section on death ineligibility, requires  -- is --is a section designed to show death ineligibility based on newly developed evidence, when the Chapter 64 test for who should get evidence doesn't consider that same scope of evidence, the right to file the chap -- the subsequent habeas petition remains illusory.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: Ms. Fisher, can I bring you back to standing?  So you sued the DA  -- I just want to make sure that I understand exactly what you want out of this. Is it your position that the DA  --even though the decision whether to give DNA evidence is discretionary when made on the part of the DA, is it your position that a declaratory judgment would influence that judgment because the DA takes  Article 64 into account in making  that decision, even if it doesn't bind him, that he would take it into account and it would be a factor, and so, if it were unconstitutional, it would be taken out of the bundle of factors that might influence the DA's discretionary decision?  Is that your position?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: I believe -- I  --if I'm understanding Your Honor correctly, yes in the sense that it's not that it would influence them but that the reasons they have cited are tied in to the unconstitutional  --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: "They" have cited? The DA has cited?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: The reasons Respond --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: Because you sued the DA. This can't be about the Texas courts.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: The reasons the Respondents have cited in their merits brief are  -- are -- for not turning over the evidence are not simple recalcitrance. They didn't simply say, well, we really just don't want to turn over the DNA. They cited reasons that were found within the statute. And if those reasons, those statutory reasons, were found to be unconstitutional, we  believe that the District Attorney's Office wouldn't rely on those.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: So it would be the equivalent -- you sought an injunction  initially, as you told Justice Kagan, trying to get the  DNA evidence. That's off the table.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Yes.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: Now, if we imagine this as an injunction, it would be an injunction enjoining the DA from taking account of the merits reasons that you say he cites, which really kind of go back to Article 64?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Well, it always goes back to Article 64, Your Honor, because of the discretionary nature. And I --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: But Article 64 is a jurisdictional provision that binds the court. So I'm trying to tie up -- you have to have a redressability argument to the DA. And in Reed, I think that's the way to understand Reed, that it was going to the DA's discretionary determination that the DA could not consider  -- all of this is assuming at the pleading stage, right, that the DA, if it was unconstitutional, couldn't take that into account even if it didn't bind him because it was an unconstitutional reason in the same way, say, race would be an unconstitutional reason. So I am trying to figure out what you want out of the DA.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: It's the same thing in Reed. The reasons that they're saying they won't turn over the  -- the DNA now are also based on unconstitutional reasons. The  --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: Article 64?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Not in its entirety. The procedures that barricade the right to develop the habeas separately --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: Does the DA have to consider Article 64?  Could the DA deny evidence for reasons entirely apart from Article 64?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: I would say no, Your Honor, because the whole purpose of a 1983 is to prevent state actors from acting in ways that violate constitutional rights. And if a provision -- if a federal court found that provisions in 1983  --I'm sorry, in Chapter 64 were unconstitutional and violated due process and the district attorney decided to rely on those same unconstitutional issues  --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: No. No, no, no, no, no. I said not -- I  --the question that I asked you was could the DA deny access to the  DNA evidence, just putting Article 64 entirely aside, just saying, listen, I don't believe in giving DNA evidence, you can go to the court and try to get it, but it's the policy of this office not to hand it over.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Yes, the DA could here, and the DA could in Reed as well.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: BARRETT
text: Okay.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: But would that defeat standing?  I mean, what  -- I don't understand that to be an argument for you not to be able to press forward in this situation where the DA, you say, has relied on 64.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Exactly. If they were to just simply say we're not turning it over, that wouldn't impact our standing in this case. That's the argument that Reed's  --that the district attorney in Reed made to this Court both in oral argument and briefing. Reed -- the  --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: And it seems to be the argument that is propelling the Fifth Circuit here. In other words, to the extent that there are other bases for the DA to deny this evidence, it's not redressable. That's  what I sort of understood to be the core of their analysis, and I -- I'm worried about that.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Absolutely. And, again, that's why 1983 is the right tool for this, because, if they're going to rely on reasons other than Chapter 64, a constitutional version of Chapter 64, to deny evidence, well, then that's basically the argument that  --that the district attorney in Reed brought to this Court and this Court rejected. The district attorney in Reed briefed and argued that a declaratory judgment will not make it more likely that they will turn it over. They will not --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: Because there were these other reasons.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Yes.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: JACKSON
text: And the Court said that's not -- in this situation  --I mean, I  -- let me just go back to your initial statement about whether or not you see Reed as setting up a new test or just re-articulating redressability as it has traditionally been understood. I thought that was the case, that Reed was not suggesting that now redressability is evaluated based on a determination of how likely it is that the person will actually get the relief that they are seeking, meaning there are no other bases that would preclude them from getting that relief. Am I right about that?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: You are right, Your Honor. And the -- the position that we've taken is that Reed doesn't change the test. We believe that it's the Fifth Circuit and Respondents who are arguing that Reed somehow created this higher bar and that now you have to do things you didn't have to do before to show standing. But our position is that when you apply Reed as it's written, we fit exactly under that category because it's the Chapter 64 reasons, as it was in Reed, that are the reasons the district attorney are denying access to the evidence. And if they applied a constitutional  version of the statute, then they couldn't rely on those same reasons. They would eliminate those reasons.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAGAN
text: But, if I could go back to, I think, the  -- the --the thrust of Justice Barrett's question, I mean, suppose that the DA here said, you know, notwithstanding what anybody says about Chapter 64, we're just not turning this over, you know, and pounds the table 10 times so you know that they're serious. Does that defeat your standing?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: May I answer, Your Honor?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Sure.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: That would not defeat standing because the declaratory judgment would still have the res judicata effect of binding the party to the determination that the statute was unconstitutional. We could then go to the state court and argue that they would have to respect that declaratory judgment. And so we would have a mechanism, and the declaratory judgment would be the key to that mechanism because that's what would change, to use the words of Reed, the legal status between the parties. It's the binding effect of the declaratory judgment in  state court that could get around their recalcitrance by simply saying we just don't want to turn it over.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: If your theory is correct, are you saying that -- are you looking for a requirement that the government  exercise discretion in light of this evidence or say they don't have any discretion but to grant relief?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: No -- we're not looking for something to force or compel the district attorney to turn it over. The declaratory judgment just doesn't have that power. But that doesn't -- that doesn't defeat Article III  standing, and it doesn't --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Well, I guess my question was, it  --it could, though, couldn't it?  I mean, if the district attorney said, look, the way I see the case, the way the evidence looks at it, this DNA evidence is not going to have any effect whatever, and if it's not going to have any effect whatever, that's not enough to get standing. Standing may not require much, but it requires something.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: If they were saying that based on  --not on Chapter 64 reasons, well, that wouldn't implicate the standing in our -- in our lawsuit to -- to declare Chapter 64 -- certain provisions of Chapter 64  unconstitutional because our 1983 puts Chapter 64 at the center of the unconstitutional  actions.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Thank you. Justice Thomas?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: THOMAS
text: Is Texas required to have a -- constitutionally to have a procedure like Chapter 64?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: No, Your Honor. There's no substantive right to DNA testing.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: THOMAS
text: So, if it was completely discretionary, what would your case look like?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: You mean if Chapter 64 didn't exist?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: THOMAS
text: Was completely discretionary with the -- with the DA.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: And if -- if Chapter -- if the ability to turn over DNA evidence was completely discretionary to the district attorney, we would have to rely on what the district attorney would do.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: THOMAS
text: So how is it any different now where the court has said that you  have not complied with the requirements, the other requirements of Chapter 64?  The CCA?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Because the CCA has never considered if we should get testing under a version of the statute that cures the constitutional infirmity found by the district court.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: THOMAS
text: So it's a constitutional infirmity in a procedure that's not constitutionally required.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Well, once the State of Texas chooses to give that right, then due process attaches.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: THOMAS
text: So what  -- what's your objective?  What do you ultimately intend to show with the DNA?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: What we hope to show with the DNA is that if we combine DNA with our other newly developed evidence, that the court will find that we make  --that the CCA will find that we make the threshold showing under 5(a)(3) that Mr. Gutierrez is death -ineligible. We may not win that.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: THOMAS
text: Because?  He's death-ineligible because?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Because he wasn't a major participant in the crime, because he didn't actually kill, attempt to kill, or anticipate a life would be taken. And he does -- and he doesn't meet the --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: THOMAS
text: So how would it show that?  How would the DNA show that?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: The DNA would be one component because the -- the  --Texas's theory in this case is that Mr. Gutierrez was not inside the house initially and didn't intend for anyone to get hurt. They admitted this in their penalty phase --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: THOMAS
text: But Mr. Gutierrez said he was in the house.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Yes. Well, the DNA would also show that that  -- that statement which he has maintained is  -- is not true. It would -- it would bolster that argument that he's been making. But, if I may, Justice Thomas, and I  -- I -- I say this respectfully, we don't have to show that we would ultimately win that lawsuit. That's not required to show that we have standing.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Alito?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: What if it were absolutely -- if it were absolutely clear that a  decision that Chapter 64 is unconstitutional in the way the district court found would have no effect whatsoever on the district attorney? Would you have standing?  Would you satisfy redressability?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Yes. And, again, that's the position the district attorney took in Reed because the binding effect --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: Well, how would it be  --how would you satisfy redressability?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Because the binding effect of the declaratory judgment would allow us to go back into state court and ask the state court to give effect to the determination of the federal court that Chapter 64 is unconstitutional in the way that the procedures block the ability to develop a subsequent habeas petition.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: So you just  -- you think you have standing because a -- a declaratory judgment would do you some good even though it would have no effect whatsoever on the district attorney who was the defendant in this case?  That's your position?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Yes, because it -- it would be a tool that we would use in the state proceedings under a new Chapter 64 motion, which is no different than Rodney Reed. It's  --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: What if you had sued the mayor of Brownsville?  We're suing the mayor of Brownsville because we think that  -- that my client's due process rights were violated by the denial of DNA testing. A declaratory judgment there that that was unconstitutional would give you the same weapon you want here.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Well, we wouldn't  -- we would have a traceability problem then, Your Honor, because the mayor wouldn't be involved in denying access to the evidence that we need. So we would fail Article -- sorry, prong 2 of the standing test in Your Honor's hypothetical.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: What if the district attorney held a news conference and he swore  on a stack of Bibles that a declaratory judgment -- that the declaratory judgment that you want would have absolutely no effect on my decision to turn over DNA evidence because I agree with the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals that it would not influence the decision on death  eligibility. Plus, I also agree with the trial court that all of this was done for purposes of delay. Would you have standing?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: If that was simply a declaration made by the district attorney, we would -- if the statute were to be found unconstitutional, because we would still have a right to take the constitutional version of the statute as declared by the federal court and the res judicata effect, that it would bind the parties to that determination, to state court. And that's exactly the position that Rodney Reed is in.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: Let me just take you back briefly to the questions Justice Thomas was asking about the DNA evidence. The most that you could possibly show from this DNA evidence -- and correct me if I'm wrong because you know the facts of this case inside out and backwards. I don't. But I  gather that what you want to prove with the DNA evidence is that other people were in the home.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: With the DNA evidence, we'd want -- that's correct.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: Okay. How would that make your client death -ineligible?  How would that tend to show that he's death -ineligible?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Because  --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: Suppose somebody else was  -- suppose that you get -- it wouldn't be surprising if you found Cuellar's DNA on  -- on  -- on some of this, right?  He found the -- he  -- he found the victim. Anyway, suppose you can prove other people were there. How does that help your client?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Because, to show that Mr. Gutierrez is death -ineligible in a 5(a)(3) subsequent habeas, we have to show two things. We'd have to show both that he wasn't in the house, and the DNA would help with that, but we also have to show his role as one that was not a major participant, and --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: Well, the DNA can't show that he wasn't there.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: And that  --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: At most, it could show that  other people were there.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Yes, but that would be one component. And that's exactly why a test in Chapter 64 that limits the evidence to the record evidence isn't looking at the right that's being squelched when, in 5(a)(3), you can present both types of evidence. And, again, Your Honor, we wouldn't have to actually show, to show that we have redressability and standing, that we're going to win the subsequent habeas.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: No, I understand that, but  I'm just wondering how long has -- this litigation has been going on for more than 25 years, right?  I mean, how much  --I just am interested in knowing whether it's going anywhere.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Although it may feel that way, Your Honor, Mr. Gutierrez filed for his first Chapter 64 motion before his federal  habeas in 2011. He has done nothing but utilize the procedures offered to him by the Texas courts. When he filed a second motion in 2019, after current counsel came on, there were  substantial factual and legal changes in Chapter 64 that led him to file a second Chapter 64 motion, including the at-fault provision from Chapter 64, which was one of the reasons he wasn't allowed to have testing. That was removed. So the law changed and the facts changed. One of the reasons that he was denied testing is he wanted testing  --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ALITO
text: All right. I  --I understand. Thank you very much.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Thank you.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Sotomayor?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: I'm trying to break this case down in my own head, so can I take it a step at a time?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Please, Your Honor.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: There were, I think, scrapings under the fingernails of the victim.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Yes.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: There was a hair that was entwined in her finger or somewhere on  -- on  --on her body.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Correct.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: There were other things that suggest that DNA testing might not just show that Mr. Cuellar was there but might show that both Garcia brothers were there, correct?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Not only is that correct, the CCA found in two  --2011 that if the DNA in those highly probative biological materials that were covered  --recovered for the very purpose  --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: That they weren't Mr. Gutierrez's.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: If that  -- yep.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: All right. I don't want to eat up a lot of time on this. But, if the evidence were to show that the other two were present, then that would give some support to your client's claim or would support your client's claim that he wasn't the one who entered the apartment to do the killing?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Yes, Your Honor.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: All right. So, putting that aside, you answered  -- I --I'm not sure what your answer was to Justice Barrett or to Justice Thomas. The Texas Code of -- Article 64.03 permits the court to order forensic testing.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Oh. That  --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: So the court could order the DNA -- could order the DA to do it, correct?  It chose not to here. You asked for injunction.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Yes, yes.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: So -- so --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: If that was a cure, yes.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: -- so you had standing. It is a right given to you under Texas law to go in and ask for an injunction,  so you had standing to do that?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Yes.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Answer my questions, okay?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Yes.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: You didn't win, but you didn't win because you continue, I think, to argue two points. One, that you can seek testing for just death eligibility. And  the district court said you're right, you don't have to prove that you were actually innocent of the crime. You just have to prove that you were  not eligible or not guilty of the death penalty, correct?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: No, Your Honor. The  -- the previous  --the -- the unconstitutional version of Chapter 64, under which Mr. Gutierrez filed for DNA testing, only allows it to go to whether or not you're actually innocent. It didn't allow you to test to show that you were death-ineligible.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: That's my point. All right. So  --but there's a second component to your due process, that this declaratory judgment, you say, includes  --I'm not quite sure how  --but that includes -- by the way, before I go on to that, Justice Thomas asked you about is there a constitutional right to DNA testing. Osborne and Skinner say that there's a constitutional right if the state elects to give you testing, correct?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Exactly. The  --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: So that was Justice Kavanaugh's first question to you, that once they elect to do it, then you have the right to have a constitutional version of it, correct?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: That's exactly correct, Your Honor.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: All right. And you claim it's not constitutional for two reasons. One, as it's been construed or as applied by somebody, okay, that it doesn't permit death eligibility. And, two, it doesn't permit new evidence to show that you're not -- that you're innocent of the death eligibility, correct?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Those are two components of the same due process violation. And the reasons they're two components of the same due process violation is because the due process violation encompasses the ways Chapter 64 limits access to the testing, because Chapter 64  --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: So let me go back there, okay?  Slow down. I'm not trying to hurt you. I'm trying to clarify things, okay?  (Laughter.)

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Justice Gorsuch asked you why the statement by the TCCA that says, even if we spot you, they said, our  statute can reach just death eligibility, the record evidence would still make you liable. And you're saying that's not true because the new evidence would show that you are not death-eligible, correct?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Correct, Your Honor.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: And what you're saying, I think, is that that issue is the issue that hasn't been looked at by the DA.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: I see what you're saying, Your Honor. Yes, that's correct.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: So that if you go back to the DA with this wealth of new evidence which he hasn't really looked at and he says to you, even if I spot you the new evidence, it's not convincing for A, B, and C reason, you might lose, correct?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: We -- well, he could certainly say that, and then we would file a Chapter 64 motion  --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: And -- and contravene that, you would have standing to say he's wrong about that.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: That's right. We would ask the court to determine if we would be eligible for testing with the new evidence.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Exactly. And so then you would still come back into court and you could then ask the court for that injunction again?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Yes, that's correct.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Looking at the new evidence?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Yes, exactly.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: All right. Thank you.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Yes.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Kagan? Justice Gorsuch?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Ms. Fisher, sorry to belabor the point, but there's a hypothetical we've been kind of dancing around in a lot of the questions, and that is let's suppose that the record were entirely clear that the district attorney and the TCCA would have multiple other grounds on which to deny relief even assuming Article 64 -- Chapter 64 applied to  death eligibility. Would -- would it be redressable then?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: It depends if those other grounds were wrapped up in the due process violation or not. And the issue --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Let's say they aren't, okay?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Oh --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Undue delay, for example, wouldn't be wrapped up in anything, okay?  So let's just hypothesize again there are multiple independent grounds. Redressable?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: If -- well, our injury would still be redressable in federal court. We would just lose in the --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: How  --how is that?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Well, because we wouldn't know if it was for undue delay until --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: No, no, let's say we know. That  --you're fighting the hypothetical, counsel, a little bit. We know. Let's just hypothesize that right now we would know that there are multiple independent grounds on which your  --your request would be denied that are independent of the thing you're complaining about. Redressable?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: I'm trying to imagine Your Honor's hypothetical with the undue delay example.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: It's an example.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: If that determination were made at the time of the filing of the new motion under the constitutional version, then we would lose at the  --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: I'm saying we know. Let's say the -- that the district attorney and the trial court in  -- in Texas has said 17 times -- just hypothesize with me -- that even if Chapter 64 applied, there's undue delay here, wouldn't be entitled to anyway, end of case. And let's say I have six other independent reasons. Just hypothesize with me. I wouldn't think that there would be redressability in that case if we knew those facts to be so.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: If the independent reasons were not part of the due process violation, then Your Honor would be correct.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Thank you.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Kavanaugh?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: A few questions. First, on how long this has been -- been going on and just the history, my understanding is, in 2015 and for several years, Texas did not oppose the DNA testing. Is that  under -- is that correct?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: That's correct, Your Honor. Mr. Gutierrez filed a -- a -- a motion with prior counsel that was entitled Motion for Miscellaneous Relief, where the only thing that we asked for in that motion was DNA testing to basically show he was death-ineligible. At that time, District Attorney Saenz wrote a  -- a two-page response and said that because of how severe and important these issues are, they would not oppose testing.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Okay. Second, on the question raised by Justice Thomas -- and Justice Sotomayor touched on this -- they could have a completely discretionary system, but if you have a system that sets up a right, then they have to have fair procedures. That's Osborne and Skinner, right?

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Absolutely. Just because a procedure didn't exist, if the state chooses  to give that right and there's a liberty interest, then they must provide due process.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Yeah. And then, third, Justice Barrett's questions, which I think are the prosecutor as defendant  -- and this goes back to my first question  -- that -- that's the awkwardness of Osborne and Skinner. It's very unusual. Reed tried to do the best it could with that without  --if you -- Reed went the other way. It totally eviscerates Osborne and Skinner, I think.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: Absolutely.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: I mean  -- but that leads to some awkward questions about what the prosecutor will do. And I just don't think -- this is more something to react to  -- I don't see how we can say something's not redressable just because the prosecutor is going to say I'm not going to comply with a court order. You know, if President Nixon said, I'm not going to come turn over the tapes no matter what, you wouldn't say, oh, I guess we don't have standing to hear the executive privilege case. I mean, it just doesn't -- it doesn't work, I don't think, to say a recalcitrant defendant can defeat redressability in that way.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: My reaction  --

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: I assume you agree with that.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: My reaction is I could not agree with you more, Justice Kavanaugh.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Yeah. On the other grounds, if there are other grounds, those probably go to the merits, but, I mean, that's  --that's what we have to figure out here down the road. You could lose down the road because there might not be a procedural due process problem. If there is a procedural due process issue with the statute, you may not win -- the DNA testing might not show.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: Anne E. Fisher
text: We might not. We may not win DNA testing.

case_name: Ruben Gutierrez, Petitioner, V. Luis Saenz, Et Al., Respondents
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: And then, on the DNA testing, just to get to this on Justice Sotomayor's questions because I think this is  -- there is  -- if --if Cuellar, Garcia, and Gracia, if I have the names correct --

text: Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  The district court's declaratory judgment did not redress Mr. Gutierrez's injury, which is the denial of access to DNA testing evidence. But, here, it would not. Unlike in Reed, here, there are several independent state  law grounds that the prosecutor has relied on to deny access to the evidence, and those grounds are unaffected by the district court's narrow declaratory judgment here. This case may also be moot, and we know that not through supposition or through speculation but because, after Mr. Gutierrez obtained that judgment, he took it to state court and tried to use it as a basis to compel District Attorney Saenz to hand over the evidence. But, because of those independent state law grounds grounded in Chapter 64, he refused, and the Court of Criminal Appeals upheld that decision for a third time. That means the declaratory judgment will not and did not redress his injury. Gutierrez responds by first redefining the scope of his injury in fact and then attempting to refashion the scope of the district court's narrow declaratory judgment. But neither can establish jurisdiction. From his operative complaint right through his opening merits brief in this Court, Mr. Gutierrez has consistently defined his  injury as the denial of access to DNA testing. And his attempt in reply to refashion the scope of the district court's declaratory judgment is contrary to that -- the letter of that judgment at J.A. 61A. And it's all -- and the CCA has already rejected that. Because the Court lacks jurisdiction twice over, it should affirm. And I welcome the Court's questions.

speaker: GORSUCH
