case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: Yes.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: -- objecting, not a store.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: Exactly right, Justice Sotomayor.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: And it was a child saying:  I don't have -- I shouldn't be barred from viewing indecent materials because adults shouldn't, correct?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: That's correct.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: And so the only rule there was what level of scrutiny do you apply to a law that applies only to children, correct?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: That is exactly right.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: And what the Court said is what's indecent for an adult could be obscene, basically, for a child. We  -- and obscene materials only have to -- for children  --obscene or indecent materials only have to satisfy rational basis?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: That's right. And I would just note that Justice Brennan's for the  -- Justice Brennan's opinion for the Court was exceptionally clear about what you were just going through, Justice Sotomayor, what was and was not being addressed.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: So, in terms of Ginsberg being a precedent, it's not a precedent involving a burden on adults?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: Yes. And our challenge is solely on behalf of adults. We are not invoking the rights of minors for purposes of our challenge.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Sable was a case in which there was a burden on children and a burden on adults. The Court applied rational basis to the burden on children and explicitly applied strict scrutiny to the burden on adults, correct?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: Yes.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: So we have direct precedent that says you'll apply different scrutiny to each age category.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: That's right. And I would just note that in Reno, Justice O'Connor's separate opinion there differentiated, just as Your Honor's suggesting, between the rights of minors versus the rights of adults, which were separately addressed in that opinion too.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Thank you.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Kagan?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: No.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Gorsuch?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: I had thought Ginsberg was a conviction of an adult who sold to minors, and it wasn't a  minor asserting any rights. It was -- he was charged and convicted of a crime knowingly selling to minors, right?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: Forgive me for agreeing with both you and Justice Sotomayor.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Yeah. I  --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: The challenge  --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: But only one of us can be right.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: Well, here's  -- here's how I -- I square the circle. It was a challenge by the seller, invoking the rights of minors. So that was what the Court was presented with.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: It was invoking his right to sell to minors.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: Justice Gorsuch, I --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: He was convicted of a crime for knowingly selling to minors, counsel.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: As Your Honor knows, in the  --in the First Amendment context, the overbreadth  -- avail --the availability of the overbreadth challenge can invoke the rights of  others. And that's exactly what I understood, per Justice Brennan, the  --the challenger there to have done  --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: All right.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: --invoking the rights of the minor.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Okay. You agree he was challenging his criminal conviction for knowingly selling --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: I -- I'm not going to disagree with --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: You can't  --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: --the procedural march, Your Honor, just -- just the substance.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: All right. And your distinction of Ginsberg is, there, he didn't have to check every ID?  Is that your  --is that your distinction?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: Correct. Liability arose from a knowing sale.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: So you think that a law that would require brick-and-mortar stores to check all IDs would be impermissible?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: I think it would be subject to strict scrutiny potentially. If the adult shows the sorts of burdens that we have here, then I think  --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: And you would argue that  --undoubtedly, that it chills and, therefore, it's a problem, right?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: Justice Gorsuch, my arguments would not be anywhere near as strong. I don't envision any such challenge, and I don't know of any such challenge being brought. I'm not suggesting the Court should write its opinion here in a way that invites those challenges.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: And with respect to age verification online, which you  -- you treat as a different kettle of fish, gambling, age ID is required by a lot of states.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: If it's not involving expression -- protected expression, I'm not  bringing a First Amendment challenge.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Okay. Applying to get a gun, Second Amendment, got to do that online?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: Different standard. We're not concerned  with chill in the same way. We don't have all the precedents that call for  strict scrutiny when you have burdens on adults and  -- and the concerns that are operative here.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: To vote in some states, you have to show an ID, a government -issued ID?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: We're not suggesting that's at issue here.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Okay. All those are okay, but this is different?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: Your Honor, it is different, and I think part of it's because of the Internet, part of it's because of the law, and part of it's because we're talking about a content-based burden on the speaker.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Okay. And then we do have an amicus, you know, from the age-verification providers saying that this can be done now online, anticipating it talking about Justice O'Connor's very thoughtful  concurrence in Reno saying this technology is going to change, and they say it indeed has changed. And you point out that we don't have much of a record given that this is on a PI. What do we do about that?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: I think it was incumbent upon the Texas legislature to make a record and show that it was wrestling with these considerations.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Or  -- or --or is it incumbent upon the challenger to the law, especially in a facial challenge, to make the record?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: I think, under strict scrutiny, it's Texas that bears the burden. It is a content-based burden on expression. You have the instruction of this Court that was clear as can be in Ashcroft and no consideration by the Texas legislature about content filtering. So I think that gives us likelihood of success out of the gate. But I would also note, Justice Gorsuch, as found by the district court, we showed that age verification, as implemented by H.B. 1181, will chill and will be invading privacy. One last point. This is a one-third trigger. And what Your Honor's positing is a more targeted law, a more tailored law that says:  Here's a particular concern, and we're  regulating according to that.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: And then what do you do about our statement in Moody that those who bring facial challenges have an especially hard row  -- not road -- row to hoe? (Laughter.)

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: Yes. We think we  -- we've -- we've done what Moody's would require any First Amendment challenger to do. We've shown that the heartland applications are unconstitutional, particularly when it comes to lack of tailoring. As you expand beyond these particular challengers who are the avowed targets of the law, the analysis only gets worse for Texas. We don't read Moody's to have transformed First Amendment jurisprudence so that you can never bring a First Amendment challenge when you're dealing with certain  unknowns and a wide array of speech that's being regulated.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Thank you.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Kavanaugh?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: On Justice Sotomayor's questions about what's before us, is it just whether we apply heightened scrutiny, do we go on to apply heightened scrutiny, you, in your opening, asked us to restore the preliminary injunction. In order to restore the preliminary injunction as you are asking, we have to make an assessment of likelihood of success on how the standard is applied, not just what the standard is, correct?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: Correct, Justice Kavanaugh. So I'm  -- I'm --but I'm respectfully making that ask of the Court, but we recognize you could stop short.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Okay. And do you dispute the problem that Texas is targeting of children's access to pornography?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: We don't dispute the underlying problem. We support efforts to solve the problem  --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Do you  --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: --as long as they're properly tailored.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: -- do you dispute the societal problems that are created both  short term and long term from the rampant access to pornography for children?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: Justice Kavanaugh, that is a complicated question that I -- I don't know that I can speak to definitively. I would say this. I think that there's a discussion, a robust discussion and a healthy discussion, about whether all sorts of things involving screens and the Internet and social media and interactions over the Internet , whether those are unhealthy for children.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Okay.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: And we understand that this is part of that discussion. I just don't think it's confined, as Your Honor was suggesting with the court -- with the question, to pornography.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: And then thinking back to Ashcroft 20 years ago versus now, age verification technology has become cheaper, more effective in preventing circumvention. At least that's what is represented to us. Do you dispute that?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: I think that the technology has evolved. We don't dispute that. I think the forms of age verification that are built into the law are absolutely susceptible to cheating because you can get the supposed proof of age --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: The question was whether it's improved since the time of Ashcroft.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: I think that it has improved, Justice Kavanaugh. I don't know that it's fit for purpose, but it has improved.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: And then European countries, France and others, are requiring age verification for this kind of thing?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: Your Honor, they have explored it. I would note that the U.K. has actually suspended age verification pending technological developments. And they do not  -- to the extent that they require age verification, the way that they're doing it looks fundamentally different from Texas  because, as Your Honor knows, Europe builds in all sorts of ferocious privacy protections and penalties if there are violations.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: That's a fair point there. On the -- on the change in technologies, how do we evaluate the ubiquitous nature of smartphones that did not exist at the time of Ashcroft?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: I think it tells you that this law is not going to accomplish its aims because a smartphone can access the foreign websites. It can access  --you can use VPNs at the click of a button to make it seem like you're not in Texas. You can go through the search engines. You can go through social media. You can access the same content in the ways that kids are likeliest to do. And H.B. 1181, by its design, does nothing, I do mean nothing, to address that.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: And, again, I'm asking those questions because you are asking us to restore the preliminary injunction, and, therefore, we need to have some sense of those questions.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: I appreciate the questions.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Yeah. And, last, on stare decisis, because that's been raised  appropriately, how do we think about stare decisis with a case like Ashcroft as to its evaluation of the facts on the ground as opposed to its legal standard articulation?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: I think Ashcroft was exactly on point because it was predictive. It was not the Court saying definitively that here is the -- the way of the world for all time and in a way  --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Do you think it's permissible for the Court to say, you know, looking at it now, with the technology as it's evolved with the smartphones, with the experience of the problems caused by children's access to pornography, that we now essentially agree with Justice Breyer's evaluation of how to apply this standard?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: Respectfully, no, Justice Kavanaugh, because of the --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: And why is that?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: Because of the posture we're in. We're here on a preliminary injunction that is  --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Likelihood that we would agree with Justice Breyer.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: Well, but, Justice Kavanaugh, I think the district court has work to do, as reflected in its undisturbed, unchallenged, well-substantiated findings about what the record says about these --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: But you agree, to  --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: --questions right now.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: -- to restore a preliminary injunction by this Court, we would have to find that you have a likelihood of success on how whatever level of scrutiny is applied, correct?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: I have a friendly amendment to t hat. You would find that the district court did not abuse its discretion by so concluding preliminarily in predicting likely success based upon a preliminary record. That's exactly what Ashcroft addressed. That's exactly what Your Honors have before you in this case.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAVANAUGH
text: Okay. Thank you very much.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Barrett?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: A question about the level of scrutiny. So this law is a little bit  -- well, there are significant differences between the way this law works and the way the law worked in Ashcroft II. And we all agree, and I -- I understood you to concede earlier, that a minor -- that only rational basis would apply if a minor brought a First Amendment challenge to this law because the law very specifically tracks only the category of speech that minors have no right -- that -- that's obscene for minors, so that minors have no right to access, right?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: I do agree with that. I would just note, Justice Barrett, that, here, we don't know the age of the minor in question. So I could  -- I don't want to prejudice the right of a 17-year-old --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Right.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: --to say I'm being limited to the rights of a 3-year-old.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Point taken.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: But we're not here asserting any such theory.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Point taken. What I'm getting at here is, and just in thinking about whether strict scrutiny is the right standard, the law draws a line between speech that's entirely unprotected as to one class and speech that is protected. It doesn't try to infringe upon the ability of adults to get it. I understand it burdens it with the age verification, but it doesn't prohibit it. The law in Ashcroft II was content discrimination on its face because it actually made it illegal to post it, right, absent the age verification defense?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: Subject to the affirmative defense, as Your Honor says, yes.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Subject to the defense.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: So  --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Right, right, right, right, right. Yeah. I -- I agree and I  -- I'm just  --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: Yeah.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: -- exploring this with you. So this law works a little bit differently because the content-based line that it draws  --I mean, it's not altogether taking this content off the table, right?  You can still display it. Pornhub can still have its videos up. But there's  -- the age verification requirement is the burden. I guess I'm wondering if there's an argument for it not being strict scrutiny  -- not being rational basis, but maybe we should be thinking of this as the age verification requirement burdens the adult's right to access the material but in a way that's not trying to discriminate on the basis of content. I know you have to see the content in order to decide where the age verification requirement applies, but, you know, City of Austin says not every check of the billboard triggers content -- triggers strict -- strict scrutiny, excuse me. What do you have to say to that?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: Two points if I may. The first is what Your Honor is positing is dependent upon the premise that  they're not putting anyone out of business in preventing them from showing their content. The  record says otherwise. I mean, the costs of age verification are such that some speakers cannot continue to speak here. And -- and the second, Justice Barrett, I do agree with Justice Sotomayor's questions that in Playboy, in Sable, the Court was dealing with restrictions that were not total bans, especially in Playboy. It was just an effort to essentially say we're going to channel this expression for adults. It's still available for adults. It's just in a way  that shields minors from it. That's exactly where the Court said that the burden in that case was analyzed no differently from the ban at least for purposes of the applicable standard of scrutiny.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Okay. Thanks.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Jackson?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: And in addition to those cases, don't you also have Reno?  I mean, I guess I don't understand how Justice Barrett's hypothesized standard would  -- would be consistent with what we said in Reno, where we said, in order to deny minors access to potentially harmful speech, the law at issue there effectively suppresses a large amount of speech that adults have a constitutional right to receive, and, therefore, it received strict scrutiny. Right?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: That's right, Justice Jackson.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: The other thing I was pretty surprised about was your concession to Justice Kavanaugh that we have to be evaluating the likelihood of success. I don't really understand that in this circumstance. I thought we had a district court that issued a preliminary injunction and a court of appeals that you say erroneously stayed it. I don't know why, if we determine that the court of appeals applied the wrong standard and vacate its ruling, the district court's injunction doesn't just come back into effect. I don't  -- you're not asking us to issue a PI, is that right?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: That's right, Justice Jackson. I just meant -- I'm sorry.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: So we're in a situation where we really don't have to be  reaching the merits of success. What we're doing, as Justice Sotomayor suggested, is  evaluating whether the court of appeals was correct when it said that this was supposed to be evaluated under the rational basis standard as opposed to strict scrutiny, right?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: Yes. All I meant to suggest to Justice Kavanaugh, that I think more guidance, rather than less, from the Court in its opinion as to why, ostensibly, the district court did not abuse its discretion would be helpful here  --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: But it may not be if they disagree with you. So what -- (Laughter.)

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: -- what -- what --I mean, this is my other question. You know, you differ from the government insofar as the government says just decide that the wrong level of scrutiny was applied here and send it back to the Fifth Circuit to apply it. You say no, we should be applying the standard for strict scrutiny. And I think that  is what is opening the door to all the questions that you're getting about whether or not this is actually narrowly tailored, whether or not there are  -- you know, content-based -- the content-filtering software is working. It's because, it seems to me, that you've asked us to apply strict scrutiny in a circumstance in which it would have been easy, as the g overnment suggests, to just say wrong standard, Fifth Circuit, and send it back.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: I never want to be disagreeing with the United States unless I must. So we don't have much disagreement with them on  -- on this, Justice Jackson. I would just note that we're talking about undisturbed, unchallenged findings by the district court and  -- and a determination that follows, in our view, inexorably from this Court's precedent. Given that there has been the detour taken by the lower court, I think  it would be helpful, I think it would be reaffirming of First Amendment --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: And the Fifth Circuit can  -- can decide on remand whether or not the district court's findings actually sustain this under the proper standard, correct?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: It can, Justice Jackson.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Finally, with respect to Ginsberg and whether or not the Fifth Circuit was correct to look at Ginsberg as the precedent that tells us what standard is supposed to apply, in your colloquy with Justice Gorsuch, he did -- and you admitted that we're talking about a person who was convicted, and he himself was an adult. But I understood the Court to have told us what the issue is. Well, first of all, the Court in the opinion says that his -- meaning the  -- the plain -- the person's contention, is the broad proposition that "the scope of the constitutional freedom of expression secured to a citizen to read or see material concerned with sex cannot be made to depend on whether the citizen is an adult or a minor."  So he was saying this is unconstitutional because it varies between adult and minor. And then the Court says:  It's enough for the purposes of this case that we inquire whether it was constitutionally impermissible for New  York to accord minors under 17 a more restricted right than that assured to adults to judge and determine for themselves what sex material they read. So, really, this was a rights -of-minors case where the person appeared to be arguing that you can't have this law because it burdens the rights of minors. So is that the situation that we have here today in this case?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: This is a fundamentally different challenge. And I disagree with you  -- I agree with you , Your Honor, that the Court was exceptionally clear in Ginsberg about adjudicating only the rights of minors in  --in the face of a challenge that it understood to be confined to the rights of minors.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: And, here, we have a challenge in which the person is saying:  Fine, whatever you do with minors, what we are suggesting is that requiring adults to do something, to do this thing, to access this material, burdens our First Amendment right. So  that's a different issue, is it not?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Derek L. Shaffer
text: Exactly right, adults and speakers. Also the  -- the websites that sponsor this content. All of which have to answer to the age-verification mandate at great cost.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: JACKSON
text: Thank you.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Thank you, counsel. Mr. Fletcher.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: Thank you, Mr. Chief Justice, and may it please the Court:  We agree with Petitioners that the Fifth Circuit was wrong to apply only rational basis review because Texas's law imposes a content-based burden on speech that is protected for adults. Our office acknowledged that strict scrutiny applied to a similar federal law  in Ashcroft II. This Court agreed. And we haven't identified a basis for applying a different standard here. Critically, though, that should not  prevent Congress or the states from restricting the distribution of pornography to children online, just as states have traditionally d one it in brick-and-mortar stores and theaters. In remanding for the application of strict scrutiny, we'd urge the Court to emphasize three points. First, the government has a compelling interest in protecting children from harmful sexual material online. Second, a law serving that interest is valid as long as it does not burden adult access more than necessary to exclude children. And, third, Ashcroft II's preliminary application of strict scrutiny 20 years ago does not prevent courts from upholding age-verification requirements today now that verification require  --has become less burdensome and experience has shown that other approaches are not working. I welcome the Court's questions.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: In the laws that you  -- that the Justice Department was arguing in favor of in Playboy and Ashcroft, in either of those, did you ever suggest or argue that there should be a lower standard?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: We did in every one of those cases before Ashcroft. In Sable, which was the first one of them, we argued for something like intermediate scrutiny under Pacifica. In Reno, which was the next one, we again invoked Pacifica and also made a Renton argument very similar to the secondary effects argument  that my friends from Texas make here. And then, in Playboy, we again invoked an argument based upon Pacifica, and Justice Breyer, in dissent, made an argument based on Renton. So we made a pitch for intermediate scrutiny repeatedly in this context. We were rebuffed. And I think that's the history that led us to concede in Ashcroft II that this was a content-based restriction that demanded strict scrutiny.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: So do you think that it's appropriate in this context of protecting children to compromise the strict scrutiny standard?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: I wouldn't describe it as compromising the strict scrutiny standard at all, Justice Thomas. But I do think it would be appropriate for the Court to emphasize that it's going to be easier for states to satisfy strict  scrutiny in this context because of the very unique nature of the interest here. Normally, the government does not have a legitimate, much less a compelling,  interest in restricting speech based on its content. That's a fundamental principle. Here, though, there's a specific category of speech defined by its content, speech that is obscene as to the minors, where everyone agrees that the state not only has a legitimate interest but a compelling interest in making sure that minors do not access that speech that is defined by its content. So I think it's going to be much easier for states to show that restrictions that are based on that content are narrowly tailored to a compelling interest.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: But will it be easy enough for this law to pass?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: I don't know about this law. We haven't taken a position on that.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: I know. But, I mean, you've been staring at this law for a long time. And  -- and -- and this law is pretty similar to 20 other laws that are out there. So you must  have some sense even if you don't want to say particularly this law.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: Yeah.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: There are 20 laws out there. Are some of them going to pass through the  -- the eye of the needle here or not?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: So let me say, if the question were framed the way Justice Thomas did, is there some version of age verification that is good enough, my answer is yes, we  --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: KAGAN
text: I'm not really talking about some imaginable version. I'm talking about, like, some version that states have enacted.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: So let me be  --give you a specific example. We defended COPA, the law this Court looked at in Ashcroft II, even after remand, in the district court, in the Third Circuit, and in the cert petition in this Court. I have no reason to think that we would come to any other conclusion about a law that looked like that today. The reason I'm hesitating about state laws is that I don't know that there's actually that much variation in the state laws. And all  of them raise some questions that we have about Texas's law that we think are questions of what  the law means that would inform the First Amendment analysis. So one is this one-third requirement. I think Petitioners say the law requires age-gating of an entire website even if it has a substantial amount of content that's protected. My friends from Texas say in the red brief that the -- if you segregate out the -- the obscene-as-to -minors content behind an age gate, you don't have to age-gate the rest of the content of the website. That seems highly relevant to us. The second one is the  --the -- the issue that my friend alluded to earlier about which methods of age verification are allowed. The amicus briefs and Texas highlight some of these newer biometric methods that seem  significantly less restrictive, but there's a question, as the colloquy earlier illustrated, whether Texas law would allow those  methods or would instead require some sort of physical  identification or transaction records of some kind. And then the last one, which has also already come up, is which minors are we talking about when we say "obscene as to minors."  I take it that the plaintiffs say that means obscene even as to the youngest minors. When we were defending a similar law in COPA, in Ashcroft II, we took the position that "obscene as to minors" means obscene as to all minors, as in inappropriate and lacking in value even as to older minors. I think the law becomes much easier to defend if Texas courts would adopt the same interpretation of the Texas law here. If I could add one thought. You know, I think that this Court has said in a series of recent First Amendment cases that tradition can be a very important guidepost in deciding both what standard of review applies and also in thinking about how to apply that standard in particular circumstances. I think, here, the tradition that applies in brick -and-mortar contexts that's reflected in Ginsberg, to be sure, but also in a  much broader family of laws that restrict the distribution of this material, as Justice O'Connor explained in Footnotes 1 and 2 of her opinion in Reno, adult theaters, adult bookstores, books and magazines, there's a long tradition of restricting this material through age-verification methods that are less formal because, as Justice Alito indicated, it's just a requirement:  Don't sell to minors. And that means that a clerk in the physical world can do it by looking at the person and only requiring ID if the person isn't obviously of age. But there's a long tradition of imposing age restrictions on the distribution of this material. So I think that supports the idea that --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: And on that point, Mr. Fletcher, I mean, that -- that -- that -- so you do take Ginsberg to be more than we're just dealing with the rights of minors. It  -- it does also impact how we think about the burden placed on people, adults, to ensure that minors don't have access. It speaks to that, as do our traditions with respect to adult theaters and many other things.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: I agree with that wholeheartedly as to the tradition that's reflected in the law  --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Yeah. Okay.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: -- that was at issue in Ginsberg. I think I read Ginsberg the same way that Justice Jackson does.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: No, I understand that. But it -- it -- it's a necessary implication of the decision.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: Right. No one thought that that law was invalid.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Right.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: I think everybody understood it's a content-based law. But everyone understands that the bur den on adults is okay  --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: And  --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: -- because requiring ID is the least restrictive way of keeping the material away from children.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: And, in Sable, there's burdens on speakers that we think are okay to protect against obscenity, right?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: Right. And the Court suggests in Sable  -- I think, there, it was a ban on the Dial-a-Porn messages, and the Court suggested some sort of age verification or something like that would be a better way to do it.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: And that would be a burden on the speaker in that.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: Exactly. Yes.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: And the same thing with adult theaters and all, so on and so forth.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: Right.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Okay. If we  --if we were to vacate the Fifth Circuit, as  -- as -- as you've suggested, there's some question in discussion about what that -- what -- what the world looks like then.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: Mm-hmm.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: Would the preliminary injunction of the district court spring back in to effect, so this law that's already taken effect will now no longer be enforceable?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: So I think that'll be a question for the Fifth Circuit in the first instance. If this Court vacates and sends it  back to the Fifth Circuit, when the Court's mandate issues, the appeal would spring back to life in the Fifth Circuit and it would be  --go back to the state of the world before the Fifth Circuit issued its opinion. The state of the world was that the Fifth Circuit had granted a stay of the preliminary injunction pending appeal. I think it would be open to the Fifth Circuit, with the benefit of whatever guidance this Court provided in its opinion, to decide in the first instance whether to reinstate that same stay pending its further consideration of the case on remand.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: GORSUCH
text: How could it do that if we've told them they've done the wrong standard?  I suppose they'd have to go back and do the right standard. But, in the interim, what happens?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: Well, I think, you know, there would be some period of time, I think it's 35 days, before this Court's mandate issues. If I were Texas, I would go to the Fifth Circuit in the meantime and ask to reinstate the stay. And I think Texas -- the Fifth Circuit should look at it with the benefit of this Court's guidance. And I note that, as the parties have informed the Court on Monday, a panel of the Sixth Circuit stayed a preliminary injunction of  Tennessee's very similar law and said that they concluded that a stay was appropriate even on the assumption that strict scrutiny applied.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: Mr. Fletcher, I share some of Justice Thomas's discomfort with watering down strict scrutiny.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: Mm-hmm.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: BARRETT
text: And I think it's common ground even with Petitioners that the state has a compelling interest in protecting minors and -- I -- I mean, I think Petitioners would be back here challenging even a different law as failing strict scrutiny, but they've left open the door to the possibility of it satisfying strict scrutiny, but, you know, come on, fatal in fact. And I  -- I think there's a sense here that the state should be able to protect minors  from some of this, but there's not a whole lot of room in the way we traditionally understand strict scrutiny for that to happen. What is your reaction to spill-over effects and whether this really would be kind of loosening strict scrutiny?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: So I -- I appreciate the concern. And I guess I'll say, just as a matter of first principles, some of your earlier questions got at wouldn't intermediate scrutiny make sense here. I have a lot of sympathy for that because, if we were writing on a blank slate, as I said to Justice Thomas, the government was arguing for something like intermediate scrutiny in this  context. So, as a matter of first principles, I think there's a lot of force to that. But we're not writing on a blank slate. We have this series of precedents. And so then I think the question is can we find room for this intuition within the parameters that the Court's decisions set. I think you can, as some of the reasons I was explaining earlier explain. This is the case where the state has a  compelling interest in restricting speech based on its content. That i s exceedingly unusual, right?  And so I think for the Court to say states have room here even under strict scrutiny, but that is because of the particular  and unique nature of the interest here, I think would give states the room that they need in this context but without watering down the strict scrutiny inquiry in other contexts where that's just not going to be true.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Thank you, counsel. In terms of the precedents that you're -- you're talking about, there are cases where the technological developments caused the Court to reconsider the precedents that were developed under, you know, not quite the horse-and-buggy days but  --but prior to very significant changes. Why -- why isn't that a pertinent factor to consider here?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: So I think it might be pertinent, Mr. Chief Justice, but the Court has also said more recently, including in NetChoice last term, that the principles of the First Amendment don't change with technology and it has tried to maintain the same fundamental First Amendment principles and apply them to new technology. And so, at least to me, all of the technological developments, which I agree are incredibly relevant to this question, fit more naturally in deciding how scrutiny applies and explaining why states are likely to able to satisfy strict scrutiny in this space than it does to revisiting what the fundamental standard for a content-based restriction on speech ought to be.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Well, the principles of the First Amendment don't change with technology, but the application of technology to the  First Amendment questions can alter the perspective in terms of what is affecting the principles and what isn't. How you apply speech protections face -to-face might be different if you're in situations where you're talking about the telephone or all sorts of other things. Historically, there have been changes in the applications of the law even if you're -- I'll correct it, the basic principles are  -- are the same.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: So  --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: And I -- and I'd just repeat one of the things that's striking about the case is the dramatic change in the technology of brick -and -mortar stores to the -- the access to pornography, which also seems to be dramatically different from what it was 40, whatever, years ago.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: So let me try answering that two ways. One is that I -- I do think there's force to the idea that there has been a lot of change, but that argument sounds a little bit like the argument that Texas and Florida made last term in NetChoice, where they said the content that's going on on social media platforms is totally different than the editorial page of the Miami Herald. That call s for a different standard of scrutiny. And this Court said:  No, we're going to keep the same standard of scrutiny but acknowledge that the application might be different because of the different facts. I think the way to be  consistent with that here would be to stick with the same standard. The second thing is, if that doesn't persuade you, I -- I think it might be a reason  to revisit the standard of scrutiny if you reach the conclusion that strict scrutiny does not give states the -- the window, the freedom, to solve this problem. We think that there is reason to believe that it does leave them that freedom, and if that's true, then I think that's another reason not to revisit precedent in this area.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Thank you. Justice Thomas?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: But you would admit, though, that we're in an entirely different world?  I mean, Playboy was about squiggly lines on cable TV.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: I don't disagree with that, Your Honor.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: And the world of Ashcroft was a world of dial-up Internet.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: Exactly. Ashcroft was worried about children accessing this material on  -- you know, at home on home computers, in libraries, in schools. Now every child has a  smartphone in their pocket with a high-speed Internet connection.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: And didn't change in technology affect our opinion from the reversal from Quill to Wayfair?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: I don't know, Justice Thomas. That -- that wasn't a First Amendment  case.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: I -- I understand that.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: So  --and I don't mean to be trying to lay down bright-line rules or to suggest that technology is never a reason when the Court is revisiting a precedent, as it was doing there. You know, here, we think Texas hasn't really squarely teed up a request to overrule precedent in the way that this Court usually expects before it takes that step. And, instead, the Fifth Circuit thought that it was applying and being consistent with this Court's precedent. We don't agree with that. You know, again, I think, if you were going to take another look at Ashcroft based on a party coming in and making a pitch to overrule it and the other line of precedent that it  --it stands on, then technological change might be relevant. Our submission here is just that you don't need to do that.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: Well, but as well as the fact that you thought that your argument in some of the earlier cases, like Reno -- you suggested a lower standard of scrutiny, and you thought it would certainly play a role here now.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: We did, you know, but, again, this Court disagreed and the record --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: Yeah, you threw in the towel, but, you know  -- (Laughter.)

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: Well, we got  --we got told no three times. (Laughter.)

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: THOMAS
text: Well, and that's just  --you shouldn't feel offended by that. (Laughter.)

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Alito?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Well, I don't want to belabor Ginsberg too much, but it is a prec edent of the Court, and do you want us -- you don't want us to overrule it, do you?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: No, not at all.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: All right. So you then have to explain why it is not very important, if not controlling, here. And what I've heard from you  -- you'll correct me if I'm wrong -- is that Ginsberg did not consider the burden on the seller or the burden on adults who wanted to purchase these magazines. Is that how you distinguish it?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: I agree with the second part. I do think it was  --as Justice Gorsuch explained, it was a conviction of the seller, but the argument he was making -- I think this is clearest on 636 to 637 of the Court's opinion  -- was children have the same First Amendment rights as adults. And the way the Court framed its rejection of that argument -- and this is a quote  -- was the law does not invade "the area of freedom of expression constitutionally secured to minors."

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Well, I -- I don't think that's exactly the argument that was actually made, and Mr. Ginsberg was represented by some very sophisticated attorneys. Here's something that they said in their brief:  "The policing problem would become an impossible burden, leading the bookseller to  abandon sale even to adults. Thus, the adults would be deprived of such literature because it was not available for distribution to adolescents."  So the argument was before the Court. The Court presumably was aware of it, took account of it in its decision, and said -- Justice Brennan's writing for the Court -- the proper standard of review here is rational basis.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: So I don't see that in the Court's opinion. I don't disagree that the parties may have put it before it, but we usually read the Court's precedents for the arguments and the issues that the Court actually decides. The other thing that I'll say is that the Court did confront arguments that were squarely framed in terms of the rights of adults that were burdened when Congress was attempting to protect minors from this material in cases like Sable and Playboy and Reno and Ashcroft and reached a different conclusion. And the last thing I'll say, you know, I mentioned to several Justices why we've argued for something like intermediate scrutiny before. As I said to Justice Barrett, I think there was force to that if we were writing on a blank slate. The reason I think we haven't argued for  rational basis review is because that would lead to results that I think even my friends from Texas would be hard-pressed to defend. Banning the speech entirely would be a rational basis of keeping it away from children. Even just in the realm of age verification, requiring you to register with the stat e to get a special card to get this material and to keep records of who is viewing what might be a rational way of keeping it away from children. But those are very hard laws to defend, and I think that's another reason why we've shied away from arguing that Ginsberg means rational basis in this space.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: I want to go back to your assertion that if we thought that the Fifth Circuit applied the wrong standard of review, we would be required to cause the preliminary injunction issued by the district court to spring back into effect. Why would that be true?  The question before us is whether we should reverse a decision that stays that preliminary injunction. So would we not have the power to reverse the decision insofar as it said that rational basis was the proper standard of review but leave it in place because we thought, hypothetically, that this law would satisfy even strict scrutiny?  Would that be beyond our power?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: Just to get the procedural posture exactly right, I don't think what's before you is a decision on the stay. What's before you is the Fifth Circuit's final decision reversing the preliminary injunction  --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Correct. All right.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: -- in this part.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Yes.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: And so, if you -- if you vacate that decision, I think normally it would return the case, the appeal, to the Fifth Circuit, and the ball would be in the Fifth Circuit's court in the first instance.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: Well, it would be -- it would return the case to the Fifth Circuit on the terms that we thought were -- were appropriate  --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: And --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: -- in returning it to the Fifth Circuit.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: And, again, I'm not -- I don't suggest the Court lacks the power to, if it wanted, to grant some sort of relief -- a stay itself. I -- I'm sure that there's a way for the Court to do that. If the Court wanted to provide guidance in its opinion, including very prescriptive guidance, I'm sure the Fifth Circuit would follow that guidance in deciding what the status quo ought be while the litigation continues.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: All right. Just so that I have them freshly in -- fresh in mind, you mentioned certain matters that you thought would be important to clarify under state law to  -- in making a judgment about whether this law satisfies strict scrutiny. Could you just tick those off again for me?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: Sure. There are three. One is the one-third requirement and whether that compels age-gating of material that is protected even as to minors if it's on a site that is otherwise covered. The second question is the permitted methods of age verification and, in particular, whether the sorts of biometric methods that are highlighted in the amicus briefs comply with Texas law. And the third is the question about, when Texas law refers to "obscene as to minors," which minors are we talking about. Are we talking about even the youngest minors, or are we talking about all minors such that material that is appropriate to older minors is prohibited?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: ALITO
text: All right. Thank you.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: ROBERTS
text: Justice Sotomayor?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: I'm not sure I understand your first point, so what do -- could you go through that again?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: Sure. So I think one of the points that Petitioners make is that the Texas law requires age -gating of a website if more than one-third of the material on that website is sexual material that's harmful to minors.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Yes.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: And Petitioners say that means we have to age-gate material even if  -- or age-gate a website even if up to two-thirds of the material is constitutionally protected even as to minors. And they say that  means that the statute isn't narrowly tailored and that it restricts speech unnecessarily. I understand my Texas  --my friends from Texas -- although, of course, the general can correct me -- to say the Texas law doesn't necessarily mean that and that a website might be able to comply by age-gating only the material that is harmful sexual material and obscene as to minors and not limiting minors' access to the other protected material. I think the law is easier to defend if you accept a construction along those lines.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: All right. With respect to the privacy -- or the -- the permitted methods of ID, counsel for Petitioner says that the more secure methods -- I don't even know what Yoti is -- but the more secure methods are prohibited by this law. Do you think that that is ambiguous?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: I don't know the answer to that.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: Mm-hmm.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: And I defer to the parties on that. I  -- I think, as petition -- counsel for Petitioners said, the Texas law seems to say that you need to have a commercially reasonable method that  -- that relies on public or private transactional data. And I think the question would be -- although, again, I welcome correction on this  -- whether something that requires  --that relies on biometric, face recognition, voice recognition, something like that, satisfies that requirement. And we just haven't --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: That's what  --

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: -- taken a position on that.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: SOTOMAYOR
text: So, to the extent that what -- whatever methods are found to be permitted under Texas law, if they have greater risk to the user, that would be part of the calculus?

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
speaker: Brian H. Fletcher
text: I do think the concerns for the user are part of the calculus, yes.

case_name: Free Speech Coalition, Inc., Et Al., Petitioners, V. Ken Paxton, Attorney General Of Texas, Respondent
